title: Listen (Rule, Prologue)
hook: the Rule's first word: listen, my son, with the ear of your heart

segments.voice: Yesterday was a block close, the end of the big questions: a family that disagrees and still says one creed. Your line was many rooms, one house. Who did you learn from, and thank? Day one thousand one hundred twelve.

Ausculta. That's the first word of a short book for monks, written in Latin by a man the church remembers as Saint Benedict. It's called simply the Rule. Before it says a thing about prayer times, or food, or sleep, or work, it says one word. Listen. Not read carefully. Not obey. Listen. And it doesn't stop at the ears on the side of your head. In the opening line, the Rule asks the reader, as a son, to listen to the teacher's instruction and to bend down the ear of the heart. We start a new block today: traditions of prayer, the different ways Christians have learned to pray. The first house we visit is the Benedictines, and their front door opens with a single word. Today's word: listen.

The ear of the heart is an odd phrase, and it's meant to be. An ear hears sounds. This ear is asked to go further in: listening that goes all the way down, that's willing to be changed by what it hears. The picture is an old one. In Proverbs, a parent says, "My son, attend to my words; incline thine ear unto my sayings." Incline. Lean the ear over, the way you lean in toward someone speaking softly in a loud room. A little further on, the Prologue reaches for a psalm, and it's a psalm about listening too: "To day if ye will hear his voice, Harden not your heart." Today. Not someday when life is quieter. Now notice what the Rule takes for granted. In its picture, God is already speaking, through scripture, through the teacher, through the community, through the day as it comes, and that the trouble is mostly on our end. We're busy. We're rehearsing our answer. We hear the first half of a sentence and fill in the rest. So the Rule doesn't start with a technique. It starts with a posture. Lean in. Bend down. Leave room for a voice that isn't yours. Prayer times, food, sleep and work all come after it. A whole way of life, built on one verb. And it's a verb anyone can practice, with or without a cloister, at a kitchen table, in a meeting, on the phone with your mother.
screen: `AN EAR THAT GOES ALL THE WAY IN.`
`TO DAY IF YE WILL HEAR HIS VOICE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to one person fully. Sit, and let your breathing slow. Bring to mind one person you'll talk with today. See their face. Now picture the conversation, and notice the moment you usually start forming your reply while they're still talking. Decide, here, that today you'll let them finish. You'll lean in a little. You'll ask one more question before you answer. If you pray, you can ask for an ear of the heart. If you don't, just hold the person in mind and rest. The bell holds the time.
Listen. The first word of Benedict's Rule: ausculta, hearing with the ear of the heart.
Your line: the ear of the heart. Today, in one conversation, let the other person finish every sentence before you start yours. Then ask one more question. Day one thousand one hundred twelve.

howItsDone: In Benedictine monasteries the Rule is read aloud to the community in short passages, and each time through it begins again with the Prologue's call to listen; lay people who follow Benedictine ways, called oblates, may read the Rule at home as well.

notes: The Rule is paraphrased throughout (no public-domain English translation on the approved list). The Latin opening 'Ausculta, o fili, praecepta magistri, et inclina aurem cordis tui' is the basis for 'listen, my son... ear of the heart'; please confirm the paraphrase.
Proverbs 4:20 is offered as the scriptural picture behind 'incline'; commentators link the opening to Proverbs. Confirm this is fair to say ('he's borrowing the voice of Proverbs').
The Prologue's use of Psalm 95 (Vulgate 94) 'today if you hear his voice' is cited as Prologue 9–10; check numbering.
'Benedictines still read from the Rule in their communities' and the oblate line in howItsDone are general descriptions not in the cited text; confirm or soften.
No date for Benedict is given, under the claims rule.
Block boundary: this opens Block B (traditions of prayer) and the Benedictine week; review picks up day 1111's carry from the index (no 1111 script was on disk when written).

Editor pass: review question now matches day 1111's carry (learn from someone and thank them); cut the Bible-heart definition (it repeats day 1120's teach) and the claim that Benedict borrows from Proverbs (now 'the picture is an old one'; myth and trapdoor softened to match); cut the unsourced claim that Benedictines still read the Rule from the spoken text.

Audit pass: the Rule's view that God is already speaking is now framed as the Rule's picture, not the narrator's claim; the unsourced 'sets the tone for everything after it' became a concrete line; howItsDone no longer garbles which text 'opens it'. Keeper: confirm the Rule is still read through in community in sequence (Rule 66 asks that it be read often).
